note: Veta knowledge cards. Each card is short, general guidance the AI may use. 'source: heuristic' means common indie practice, not a measured statistic. Never put made-up numbers in a card.

cards.title: Online multiplayer multiplies work for small teams
cards.summary: Online play touches almost every system: movement sync, enemy state, saves, UI, testing with several machines, and support after launch.
guidance: Ask whether the core loop is fun in single-player or local co-op first.
If online is essential, build the networking layer before content, not after.
Budget extra time for testing with real players on different connections.
A common cut: launch single-player or local co-op, add online in an update.

cards.title: Open worlds are a content problem, not a map problem
cards.summary: A big map is cheap to make empty and expensive to make interesting. Every area needs things to do, art to fill it and testing.
guidance: Prefer a few dense, hand-made zones over one large sparse map.
Count content per area (encounters, secrets, quests) before committing to size.
Streaming, saves and performance get harder as the world grows.

cards.title: Procedural levels: start from hand-made templates
cards.summary: Fully generated levels are hard to make fun and hard to debug. Shuffling hand-made rooms or chunks gives variety with control.
guidance: Build 10-20 hand-made rooms and randomize their order and contents first.
Add generation rules only where players notice repetition.
Keep a seed system so bugs can be reproduced.

cards.title: Content counts multiply the art workload
cards.summary: Each extra character, biome or boss is not one task: it brings models or sprites, animations, effects, sounds and balancing.
guidance: Multiply content counts by the assets each one needs before estimating.
When one artist supports the whole game, art is usually the real bottleneck, not code.
Cut a full content type (one biome, one character) rather than shrinking everything a little.

cards.title: Define the first playable before anything else
cards.summary: The first playable is the smallest build where a stranger can play the core loop start to finish once.
guidance: List only what the core loop needs: control, one goal, one obstacle, a win and a fail state.
Use placeholder art. Test whether it is fun before producing content.
Give it a date. If it slips, cut scope, not testing.

cards.title: First estimates are optimistic
cards.summary: Task estimates usually leave out integration, bugs, polish and the time between tasks. First projects tend to underestimate the most.
guidance: Keep a visible buffer instead of padding every task silently.
Compare estimated vs actual days after each milestone and adjust the rest of the plan.
If the plan only works with zero surprises, the scope is too big.

cards.title: Reserve the end of the schedule for fixing, not adding
cards.summary: The last stretch before launch fills up with bugs, platform requirements, store assets and feedback fixes.
guidance: Set a content freeze date well before launch; after it, only fixes and polish.
Plan time for store page, trailer, builds and platform review.
Keep a 'post-launch' list so good ideas have a home that is not this release.

cards.title: Playtest feedback is a common source of scope creep
cards.summary: Testers suggest features; the underlying problem is often smaller than the suggestion.
guidance: Ask what problem the suggestion solves, then look for the cheapest fix.
Act on patterns across several testers, not one loud request.
Run every new idea through Scope Guard and log the decision.

cards.title: Solo developers: one core mechanic, done well
cards.summary: A solo developer is also the artist, tester, marketer and support team, so production time is a fraction of total time.
guidance: Pick one mechanic the game is about and cut systems that do not feed it.
Use existing assets or a simple art style that you can produce consistently.
Start marketing (store page, devlog) while building, not after.

cards.title: Rage and precision platformers must feel fair
cards.summary: Players accept punishment when they understand why they failed. Unclear hitboxes, camera problems or random effects make frustration feel unfair.
guidance: Make the cause of every fall readable on screen.
Introduce twists (control changes, fake checkpoints) one at a time and telegraph them.
Design a few clip-worthy moments; this genre spreads through streams and short videos.
Test with people who did not build the game and watch where they quit.

cards.title: Branching stories grow faster than you expect
cards.summary: Every choice that changes the story multiplies writing, testing and art. Most narrative games branch and then bring paths back together.
guidance: Use branch-and-bottleneck: let choices diverge, then reconverge at key scenes.
Track consequences with a few flags rather than separate storylines.
Write a word budget per chapter and check it against the schedule.

cards.title: Cozy sims: depth of a few systems beats many shallow ones
cards.summary: Cozy games live on routine and attachment. Many half-built systems feel empty; a few rich ones feel alive.
guidance: Pick the 2-3 daily activities the game is about and make them satisfying.
Fewer villagers with real personality beat many with one line each.
Plan content for the first in-game week in detail before planning a full year.

cards.title: Put the store page up long before launch
cards.summary: Store pages collect interest over time; a page that goes live just before launch has little to show on day one.
guidance: Prepare capsule art, screenshots, a short trailer and a clear one-line pitch.
Check the platform's current rules and review times before picking a launch date.
Share progress regularly and point every post to the store page.

cards.title: Make text ready for translation early
cards.summary: Retrofitting translation is painful when text is hard-coded or baked into images.
guidance: Keep all player-facing text in string tables from the start.
Leave room in UI for longer languages.
Avoid text inside textures.

cards.title: When cutting, remove whole features, not quality
cards.summary: Trimming every feature a little leaves a game where nothing feels finished. Removing a whole feature keeps the rest polished.
guidance: Rank features by how much they serve the core loop; cut from the bottom.
Move cut features to a post-launch list and log why in the decision log.
Re-check the release forecast after each cut.

cards.title: Make effects felt, not read
cards.summary: Players skim or ignore on-screen text during action. An effect announced with text is understood but not felt; the same effect shown through camera, screen, character and sound is both.
guidance: Replace text warnings with camera, screen effects, character reactions and sound.
Test it: can a player tell which effect started without any text?
Keep an optional icon for accessibility instead of a text banner.

cards.title: Telegraph, then hit
cards.summary: Sudden changes feel random and cheap. A short build-up before an effect lets the player brace, and makes the change feel deserved.
guidance: Give each disruptive effect a short, consistent build-up (pulse, rumble, rising shake).
One shared telegraph for all effects is enough; make each effect distinct by its own sound and visual.
Ask testers: did it feel like a fair consequence or a random punishment?
cards.source: heuristic (ANGRY playtest and Veta producer review, Oct 2026)

cards.title: A quick tap must still give a useful jump
cards.summary: Variable jump height is good, but if releasing early cuts too much, tapping feels broken and the jump feels heavy.
guidance: Only allow the jump cut after a short minimum time.
Keep the cut gentle so a tap is a smaller but still useful jump.
Add coyote time and a jump buffer so near-misses on input feel forgiving.

cards.title: 3D platformers need a landing shadow and a calm camera
cards.summary: Judging depth in 3D is hard. Without a shadow under the character and a camera that follows on its own, players fight the camera instead of the level.
guidance: Put a blob shadow directly under the character at all times.
Let the camera recenter behind the player after a moment without mouse input.
Limit the vertical camera angle and keep the camera from clipping into geometry.

cards.title: Feel effects are cheap; new content is expensive
cards.summary: Screen effects, camera moves and simple particles reuse the same tools and assets, so each one is usually small work. New characters, levels, animations and voiced lines each need their own assets and are where time goes.
guidance: Do not cut feel effects to save time before checking whether they need new assets.
When estimating, separate 'tuning and post-processing' from 'new assets'.
If code is written with AI help, logic tasks shrink most; tuning, level design, audio and writing shrink least.

cards.title: Every punishing system needs an escape valve
cards.summary: Systems that make the game harder after failure can spiral: failing makes the game harder, which causes more failure. Without a way out, it stops feeling fair.
guidance: Give the player a reliable way to lower the pressure through play (recovering lost ground, a calm zone, a reset point).
Check the worst case: what happens after three failures in a row?
Introduce escalation steps one at a time so each is understood before the next arrives.

cards.title: Steam release rules set hard dates before launch
cards.summary: On Steam, a new developer cannot launch whenever the game is ready: the app fee, the Coming Soon page and two reviews each need lead time.
guidance: Pay the Steam Direct fee ($100 per game) early: Steamworks docs describe a waiting period between paying and releasing for your first titles (30 days on the Steam Direct page, 21 days on the onboarding page). Plan for 30.
A new game needs a Coming Soon page live for at least two weeks before release, and Valve asks for the store page to be submitted for review at least 7 business days before it should go live.
The store page and the release build each go through a review that takes about 1-5 days, so work backwards from the launch date and add these steps to the plan.
Wishlists build up while the page is live, so a page that goes up only weeks before launch has little to show on day one.
